doc.title: Phoebe Jacobs and Jackie Harris interviewed by Monk Rowe, Rome, New York, August 21, 2006

title: Armstrong's honesty and enduring appeal
summary: Jacobs describes the outpouring at his death, constant requests for his image and voice, and his pure honesty.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: I’ve often — people often describe Pops as a totally honest person. Is that a fair assessment of him?

I would say that you can’t be emphatic enough about that. I have often thought having Satch the day that they called me to come to the office that Louis Armstrong passed, and I sat in a room where the head of every country, the head of every country, the presidents, the governors, the outpouring for this man’s death was so outstanding that no matter how I measured him in his being vital to the world, I could never estimate how great it was. And of course the longer he lives the more I know how great he is because it’s never

stopped. Thank God it’s never stopped. Every day of my life I get at least a minimum of two inquiries for the use of something of Louis Armstrong — his face, his voice, a tape — that’s a minimum. And it comes from all over the world. But the interesting thing about this whole deal of people loving Louis is I try to analyze what is it. He wasn’t handsome by standards of handsomness, like he wasn’t a Harry Belafonte or a Sidney Poitier. He wasn’t cultured, like Denzel Washington or one of those cats. But he had something that was magic that nobody else has, and that was pure honesty. He was honest and what you saw is what you got. He didn’t care if you were president, if you were the King of England or who you were, he treated everybody the same way. He was honorable and honest and straightforward.
